subject: Cost segregation: the tax move worth understanding (when it actually works)
preheader: Front-load 25-35% of depreciation · The $4-7k study · Why it backfires on short holds

marketSnapshot.headline: Cost segregation — front-load depreciation, but know the trade
marketSnapshot.body: Cost segregation studies break a building into components — land improvements, personal property, systems — that depreciate over 5, 7, or 15 years instead of the standard 27.5 years for residential rental. The result: 20-30% of building value gets reclassified to faster schedules, front-loading meaningful depreciation deductions into years 1-5 of ownership. Real benefit for buy-and-hold investors with W-2 income to offset. Less benefit (and sometimes negative) for short-hold strategies.

dealSpotter.body: $400k rental property, 10+ year planned hold. Assume $80k gets reclassified to 5-15 year schedules. You front-load ~$50-65k of depreciation deductions into the first 5 years vs spreading across 27.5. At a 32% effective tax bracket, that's $16-21k of accelerated tax savings in those first 5 years. Cost of the engineering study: $4-7k. Net: $12-16k benefit plus meaningful time-value-of-money on the front-loaded deductions.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Math gets tight at lower property values · marginal
dealSpotter.body: $200k rental property, 7-year planned hold. The study cost ($4-7k) is a higher percentage of the deal, and the deductions reclassified are smaller in absolute terms. Net benefit might be $3-7k over the hold — real money but not a slam-dunk. The break-even is roughly $250k+ property value for cost seg to clearly win.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Depreciation recapture eats most of the savings
dealSpotter.body: $300k rental sold after 3 years. The front-loaded depreciation gets 'recaptured' at ordinary income rates when you sell (vs the favored 25% rate on standard depreciation recapture). Short holds + cost seg often produce a net wash or slight loss. Cost seg pairs poorly with flipping. Pairs WELL with 1031 (defers the recapture too).

blogFeature.title: 1031 exchange basics: how to defer capital gains on rental property
blogFeature.excerpt: Cost segregation + 1031 exchange is the tax-savvy investor's combo. Front-load deductions now, defer the recapture by rolling into the next property. The two-step tax strategy that materially improves IRR for tax-aware investors.

qa.question: Should I do cost seg on every rental I buy?
qa.answer: No — three conditions all need to be true for cost seg to clearly win. (1) Property value is high enough to support the study cost: typically $250k+ purchase price. Below that, the $4-7k study eats too much of the benefit. (2) Planned hold period is 7+ years. Shorter holds + depreciation recapture often wash out the savings. (3) You have W-2 or active income to offset the deductions against, OR your spouse qualifies as a real-estate professional and can use the losses fully. If you're in a 22% bracket with only passive rental income to offset, cost seg's benefit is much smaller than if you're in a 35-37% bracket with active income. Default rule: cost seg makes sense on rentals in the $300k+ range that you plan to hold long-term in your active-income years. Talk to a CPA — they'll model your specific numbers in 30 minutes.
